title: The (deterministic) k-server conjecture
short_statement: A 2026 preprint claims the deterministic k-server conjecture via the Work Function Algorithm.
open_problem: Verify the claimed general-metric theorem rather than treating the original competitive-ratio gap as unchanged.
background: The k-server problem generalizes paging to metric spaces. Work-function analysis supplied the longstanding general upper bound and many exact special cases. The new claim below addresses arbitrary metrics.
full_statement: Let $(M,d)$ be a metric space and let an online algorithm control $k$ servers located at points of $M$. A request sequence $\sigma=(r_1,r_2,\ldots)$ is revealed online. To serve request $r_t$, the algorithm must move one server to $r_t$ if none is already there, paying the distance moved. Let $ALG(\sigma)$ be the total movement cost and $OPT(\sigma)$ be the minimum offline cost with full knowledge of $\sigma$. The historical deterministic $k$-server conjecture asks whether for every metric space with at least $k+1$ points there is a deterministic online algorithm with $ALG(\sigma)\le k\,OPT(\sigma)+O(1)$ for all request sequences. A matching lower bound of $k$ is known, and a matching upper bound is now claimed in the paper below.
known_results: Coester, Koutsoupias, and Zbysinski, 'The k-server conjecture is true' (arXiv:2609.15979), Theorem 1.2, state that for every metric, initial configuration $C_0=\{s_1,\ldots,s_k\}$ and finite request sequence $\sigma$, $$\mathrm{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\,\mathrm{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{i<j}d(s_i,s_j).$$ Together with the classical lower bound, this claims the sharp deterministic ratio, superseding the historical $2k-1$ upper bound.

progress.summary: A full resolution is claimed in the September preprint; theorem/model and proof overview reviewed, not independently certified.

counterexample_rationale: A lower bound above $k$ would likely require an explicit metric and adversarial request distribution, but proving it against all deterministic algorithms is hard. Small-case potential failures can be machine-checked but do not by themselves refute the conjecture.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated checks may help audit the claimed potential inequalities. Success on a finite benchmark is not a universal proof.

literature.synthesis: Older work-function bounds and potential-search benchmarks are historical precursors. The new claim concerns the original deterministic problem.

reviewed.ref: Mark S. Manasse, Lyle A. McGeoch, Daniel D. Sleator, 'Competitive Algorithms for Server Problems', STOC 1988 / Journal of Algorithms 1990
reviewed.result: Introduces the $k$-server problem and the $k$-server conjecture; proves foundational lower bounds and special cases.

reviewed.ref: Elias Koutsoupias, Christos H. Papadimitriou, 'On the k-Server Conjecture', Journal of the ACM 1995
reviewed.result: Proves the Work Function Algorithm is $(2k-1)$-competitive.

reviewed.ref: Zhiyi Huang, Hanwen Zhang, 'Deterministic 3-Server on a Circle and the Limitation of Canonical Potentials', arXiv 2022
reviewed.result: Proves WFA is $3$-competitive for $3$-server on circle metrics and identifies limitations of canonical potential frameworks.

reviewed.ref: Kirill Brilliantov, Etienne Bamas, Emmanuel Abbe, 'k-server-bench: Automating Potential Discovery for the k-Server Conjecture', arXiv 2026
reviewed.result: Provides a sound but incomplete computational benchmark for discovering potential functions in special $k$-server cases.

reviewed.ref: Christian Coester, Elias Koutsoupias, Marek Zbysinski, 'The k-server conjecture is true' (2026)
reviewed.result: Theorem 1.2 is the claimed general resolution; see the What Is Known section.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Audit the new work-function potential and its treatment of arbitrary metrics and initial configurations.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A full solution must handle all metric spaces and all request sequences, or explicitly state and prove a new special case. Passing a finite benchmark is not a proof unless the benchmark is shown to imply the claimed competitive ratio for the target metric family.
